utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The accused is not present in the courtroom at this moment. Mr. Lukic, have you been informed about the reason why he is not present at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm not clear, Your Honour, what's the reason why Mr. Mladic is not in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, let me tell you what information the Chamber received. Mr. Mladic was invited to come to the Tribunal at 8.30 this morning. He then said that he wanted to continue and to finish his breakfast. Then at 9.10, approximately, he was still not -- had still not finished his breakfast, and I do understand that he is on his way now to the Tribunal. But the Chamber under the present circumstances is inclined to proceed, at least for the first session, without Mr. Mladic because preferring to finish your breakfast for more than 40 minutes rather than to come to court is considered by this Chamber to be a waiver of your right to be present, a right which is a right of an accused. If there's any further comment on that, I'd like to hear, but apparently you were not informed, Mr. Lukic, about the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I really am not in details. I just heard it from you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then assuming that this information the Chamber received through the Registry is accurate, we'll start, and after the first break, if Mr. Mladic has arrived, of course, he is welcome to further attend the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Your Honours, we are. Mr. Jeremy will be handling the next witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. No protective measures. Mr. Stojic is the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Stojic. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration, the text of which is now handed out to you by Madam Usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojic. Please be seated. Mr. Stojic, you will first -- you will be first examined by Mr. Jeremy. You'll find him to your right. Mr. Jeremy is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Stojic. Could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Grgo Stojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, do you recall testifying before this Tribunal in the case of Brdjanin et al. on the 6th and 7th of June, 2002?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I would ask that 65 ter 28453 be called up on the screens. This is a redacted copy of the transcript of this witness's testimony given before this Tribunal in the Brdjanin case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any technical problem with it to appear on our screens? There we are. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, have you recently had an opportunity to listen to an audio recording of your testimony in the Brdjanin case?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Following your proofing on the 26th and 27th of October, 2012, I understand that you wish to clarify the names of two of the victims from the incident on the 2nd of November, 1992. Firstly, I understand that at transcript page 6779, line 20, which is e-court page 19, the reference to Adlo Tadic should be, instead, to Karlo Tadic. Is that correct, Mr. Stojic?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And on line 21 on the same page, the reference to Josip Fertalac [phoen] should be to Tomika Potalac [phoen]. Is that correct, Mr. Stojic?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: It should be Tomica Potalac [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you. I also understand you that you want to make a clarification in relation to your testimony about a conversation between a Bono Tutic and a Tomo Delic concerning weapons which we'll discuss in your testimony. Specifically at transcript page 6771, line 6 [Realtime transcript read in error "67"], which is e-court page 11, you wish to insert the word "now" between the word "discussion" and the word "that" so that the sentence now reads: "Delic literally told Bono and the others that he had done this because we were friends and that there would be no further discussion now that weapons had started talking." Is that correct, Mr. Stojic?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Aside from the clarifications just made, if you were asked the same questions today that you were asked in the Brdjanin case, would you give the same answers, in substance?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, basically I would give the same answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And do you today affirm the truthfulness and accuracy of your prior testimony?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I confirm that it was truthful and accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time the Prosecution tenders the redacted version of the witness's testimony in the Brdjanin case, 65 ter 28453, as the next Prosecution Exhibit pursuant to our Rule 92 application of 28 September 2012.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I give an opportunity to Mr. Ivetic to make any submission, the reference to line 67 should be line 6, I take it, on page 6771. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection to the tender of the redacted transcript under Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you please assign a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28453 becomes Exhibit P365, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P365 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, with your leave I will now read a short summary of Mr. Stojic's written evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have explained to Mr. Stojic the purpose of doing so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: In 1992, Grgo Stojic was a Bosnian Croat farmer living in the village of Skrljevita, Sanski Most. The witness gives general evidence about the persecution of non-Serbs within Sanski Most, including Sanski Most Crisis Staff demands and radio broadcasts stating that non-Serbs must surrender their weapons. The witness describes the killing of a number of men near the village of Skrljevita on 2 November, 1992, referred to as Scheduled Incident A.7.5 in the indictment. During this attack, the witness, together with five other men from his village, were captured by four Bosnian Serb soldiers who were armed with machine-guns and who described themselves as Seselj's army. The witness and his five fellow villagers were questioned by these men, searched, and beaten. They were then lined up and shot. The witness was shot in the arm, hip, and stomach, and together with the five fellow villagers, left for dead by the attackers. When the witness regained consciousness, he realised that he was the only survivor of the attack. He later learned that four other men from this area were killed by these same attackers that same day. The witness went to Banja Luka hospital, where, after treatment, he was detained in a cell that was guarded by Bosnian Serb soldiers. There, he and other non-Serbs were beaten by Bosnian Serb soldiers and civilians on a number of occasions. The witness was finally released on 11 December 1992 and shortly after he travelled to Croatia, where he remains to this day. That concludes the summary, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, I will now ask a few questions relating to the requests made to non-Bosnian Serbs in Sanski Most and in particular in your village in Skrljevita to surrender any weapons. This is discussed in your Brdjanin testimony now in evidence as P365 at transcript page 6768 to 6771; e-court pages 8 to 11. And, Your Honours, in case it is helpful, Sanski Most municipality and Skrljevita village are identified on page 36 of the Prosecution's municipalities court binder, P00178. Mr. Stojic, in your Brdjanin testimony at transcript page 6770 to 771, e-court pages 10 to 11, you discuss three men from your village, namely, Ilija Tutic, Bono Tutic, and Ivica Tutic being called to a meeting by someone by the name of Tomo Delic together with a military officer. Mr. Stojic, who was Tomo Delic?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Tomo Delic was initially the commander of the Crisis Staff and representative of the Serb armed forces in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: At transcript page 6771, you state that Bono Tutic told you that at that meeting Tomo Delic had requested that your village surrender a number of rifles that he alleged your village had obtained from Croatia. Were you aware of your village obtaining these weapons from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: We were not aware of any weapons having been obtained, nor did we receive any.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And were you aware of Ilija Tutic, Bono Tutic, or Ivica Tutic being involved in the military in 1992?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: They had no connections to the army in 1992. Just like myself, they were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: In your Brdjanin testimony, at 67 -- at transcript page 6769, line 21, e-court page 10, you refer to the disappearance of Ivica Tutic at the beginning of July 1992 after he had been asked to report to a police station in Sanski Most. How long after this meeting with Tomo Delic did Ivica Tutic disappear?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: After the meeting, Ivica disappeared after one and a half months ago, i.e, sometime in mid-July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, if I look at my own screen, page 10 in e-court is page 6770 in the transcript pages. So, therefore, there seems to be a discrepancy between what -- because you said it was 6769 to be found on page 10 of e-court. Now which of the two would be the better solution?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: That's my mistake, Your Honours. It should be e-court page 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 9. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, I'd now like to ask a few questions relating to the events on the 2nd of November, 1992, that left you permanently disabled and resulted in the deaths of a number of your neighbours. In your Brdjanin testimony, at transcript page 6777, e-court page 17, you describe being questioned by four soldiers shortly before the execution began. In particular, you state that before the shooting started, you were each asked about the whereabouts of Ilija Tutic and Bono Tutic. Were these two of the three men the same two men that Tomo Delic met at the meeting that we've just discussed?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, those were the two men.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: In your Brdjanin testimony at transcript page 6779, line 20, e-court page 19, you describe later hearing about the death of four other men from your village that day. You refer to one of them as Bruno Tutic. Is Bruno Tutic the same man as Bono Tutic?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Bono Tutic -- or, rather, Bruno Tutic is a non-existent name. It must have been a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So the correct name is Bono Tutic, not Bruno Tutic?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'd now like to discuss briefly certain aspects of your experience in Banja Luka hospital where you stayed from the 2nd of November, 1992, to the 11th of December, 1992. Shortly after your initial treatment for your injuries, you were transferred to what you describe in your Brdjanin testimony at transcript page 6783, e-court page 23, as prison cells within the urology ward, firstly to cell number 8 and then criminal number 9. In cell number 9 you describe, in transcript page 6789, being beaten on a number of occasions by "civilians and by soldiers and by anyone who could enter that cell." Mr. Stojic, how were people able to enter that cell?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: These people could enter the cell in the following way. The guards would let them in. They would take the door handle out, and that's how they let them in.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And when you refer to "the guards," who were these guards?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: These guards were soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Was it possible to gain access to these cells without the permission of the soldier guards outside?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And were you ever attacked by one of these soldiers guarding your cell?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could you please provide details of that attack.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was attacked around day break, say, about 4.00 in the morning, by a soldier named Slobodan. However his nickname was Zuco. He beat me. He beat me up. Before that, when some of them came in, they would also beat --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, it is ambiguous. Either the witness personally or other prisoners as well, on their wounds, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, when you refer to the beatings on your wounds, were you referring to just yourself or to fellow detainees within the cell within the hospital?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: I was referring to the others as well. The others who had been detained with me. They beat up people using whatever they could lay their hands on. They would kick them, they would hit them with rifle-butts, with crutches, whatever. Everybody did whatever they pleased.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, in your Brdjanin testimony, at transcript page 6831, line 13, e-court page 63, you state that: "When I left the prison, the hospital, Mrs. Nada came to me and she helped me. She helped get me out." How did Mrs. Nada help you get out?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: This is the way it was. On the 2nd of December - or was it the 3rd of December? I do not remember the date exactly - the main nurse walked in, Slobodanka Brankovic, that's her maiden name. Her married name was Samardzija. She said that we were free, that we could go home once we paid the hospital expenses. However, on the 9th of December, a guard by the name of Dragan was on duty. He came into that room and he said that Ivo Nikic could go home because he was in cell number 8. However, I asked him to have this woman come to see me so that I could send a message to Mrs. Nada, if she could come and bring money so that I could cover expenses so that they could let us go. However, this man was confused this. This was Miroslava Grgic, also a Croat, from Poljaci [phoen]. And on the 9th of November, Mrs. Nada came to see me in this cell. We exchanged greetings in the morning and she said that everything would be all right. She went to this person, Slobodanka, that head nurse, and she sent her to the military command in Banja Luka. She spent some time there and she said that she also had lunch there with them, and then she came to me and then I was released. She took me out of hospital. Me and this Ivo Nikic as well. In front of the hospital we were met with Adolf Visaticki, a priest, and he took us to Caritas in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I interrupt you for a moment, Mr. Jeremy, just for one clarification. I would like to take you back for a moment to the situation in cell number 9 where you were detained together with other prisoners and you were asked about the beatings on the wounds, and then you said, "I was referring to the others as well." Does that mean you were beaten in the same way on your wounds by the guards? You personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could the Court Officer please bring 65 ter 07062 to our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, the document being brought up on the screen before you is a letter written by Danilusko Kajtez, whom you describe in your Brdjanin testimony as one of your attackers on the 2nd of November, 1992. In this letter, Mr. Kajtez requests for various people to intervene on his behalf in order to obtain his release from Pre-Trial detention in connection with the event that resulted in your being shot on the 2nd of November, 1992. One of the men he refers to in that letter is Tomo Delic whom you discuss at various points in your Brdjanin testimony and who we have discussed today. I'd like to go to bullet 10 on page 1 in the English version, and in the B/C/S version it's page 2 and the second asterisk. Mr. Stojic, in the paragraph on the screen before you Mr. Kajtez writes: "If you fail to get me out of here, I will say that I killed on the orders of Tomo Delic and Vlado Vrkes with the intention of resettling the village of Skrljevita as soon as possible. All of which could be easily proven in court." Mr. Stojic, the nine men killed by Kajtez and his fellow soldiers on 2nd of November, 1992, which village were they from?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: I mean all of them were from the village of Skrljevita except for these three, Zalko, Nikic Tutic, and Ivo Tutic. They are from Kruhari which borders with Skrljevita. There's just a road there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And what happened to the village of Skrljevita after these killings on 2nd of November, 1992? Briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: I mean, well, the villagers had to leave because they were being intimidated. Their property was looted. Part of the population moved to Sasenac [phoen] or to Kruhari until they all went to the Republic of Croatia. They all tried to get out in any which way. However, relatives in Croatia had to provide letters of guarantee, or rather visas, and then everybody moved out. Whoever could. And those who stayed on, well, there were killings all the way up until the end of the war there. In Skrljevita the total number of killed persons is 18, five of which are women, and there's one child too.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender this exhibit, 65 ter 07062 as the next Prosecution Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would object on the basis that the proofing statement that we were given for this witness confirms that this witness has never seen this document before. Therefore, he is not in a position to authenticate the document or to give any personal details that would lend some kind of meaning to the document. We therefore submit this document is not properly being tendered through this witness. And perhaps through the bar table or through some other witness to lay some foundation for document it would be appropriate, but under the -- under the law of the case as it has been to date, I don't believe this document is appropriate through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, the subject of the letter concerns an incident which resulted in -- in this witness being shot. The witness is aware of the man who wrote the letter. He is aware of the various recipients of the letter and men mentioned in this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask then is the Prosecution presenting this letter for the truth of the matters asserted within it? If so, I would object on that basis as well. That would be an improper attempt to introduce a written statement without going through their 92 bis, 92 ter, or 92 quater.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would this be a statement under 92 bis, 92 ter, and 92 quater? Isn't it true that it is mainly for statements which are made for the Tribunal. This seems to be of a totally different nature, or am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I understood the comments of counsel that they're -- that they're presenting the letter and what's presented in the letter as if it's being presented for truth of the matters asserted, in which case it therefore must be a statement and must comply with one of the rules that this Tribunal has for the introduction of statements. If it's being presented for that are purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider the tendering and the objections raised by the Defence and the document should be marked for identification at this moment. Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 07062 becomes Exhibit P366, MFI'd, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And keeps that status for the time being. Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, to finish I'd like to ask a few questions about the treatment that you received for your injuries and the consequences of those injuries for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could the Court officer please bring 65 ter 15709 to our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, being brought up on the screen before you is a newspaper article that details the operation that you had on your arm in Oklahoma City in the United States in October 1994, almost two years after you sustained your injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please zoom in on the photographs of Mr. Stojic which show his arm before and after the operation in the US.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, does this article and, in particular, the pictures contained within it accurately describe the operation that you had to undergo in the US for your injuries?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is accurately described.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this exhibit, 65 ter 07062 as the next Prosecution public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Forgive me, Your Honours. The 65 ter is 15709.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 15709 will receive number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P367, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P367 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, this Friday will mark the 20th anniversary of those events on 2nd of November, 1992. What impact has that attack had on the life that you have led over the past 20 years?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: That attack left an all-ought mark on me. I am disabled, 70 per cent disabled, physically, mentally. I have nightmares on account of that. Sometimes I have problems with my digestion too. I mean, I do not have any proper satisfaction. I did not receive anything financially. I can only thank the Republic of Croatia for the fact that I now have health insurance.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I have no further questions at this time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I am prepared to deal with the associated exhibits for this witness now if it's an appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's have a look at them. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, following proofing with this witness over the weekend, I'd now like to tender ten of the 17 associated exhibits for this witness. And I am prepared to list these exhibits on request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you please take them one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: The first exhibit is 06377.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 06377 becomes Exhibit P368, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P368 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: The next exhibit is 07074.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Becomes Exhibit P369, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: The next exhibit is 15705.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 15705 becomes Exhibit P370, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: The next exhibit is 15706.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Again, no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 15706 becomes Exhibit P371, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: The next exhibit is 18446.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 18446 becomes Exhibit P372, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: The next exhibit is 18447.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 18447 becomes Exhibit P373, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: The next exhibit is 18543.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 18543 becomes Exhibit P374, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: The next exhibit is 18544.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 18544 becomes Exhibit P375, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And the last exhibit is 18572.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Also no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 18572 becomes Exhibit P376, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. That was it, Mr. Jeremy?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, are you ready to start your cross-examination before we take a break in approximately seven minutes from now?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic and you'll find him to your left.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Stojic. The Defence appreciates all that you've gone through and endured and wishes to ask you some questions to get a better understanding of these events. First of all, I know that it is mentioned in your testimony and some of your statements that you did your military service in the JNA. I want to ask you was this part of your compulsory service that every male in the former Yugoslavia had to undergo at the time?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And for those that might be unfamiliar with the structure of the compulsory military service in the former Yugoslavia, could you tell us at what age, or ages, was compulsory military service mandatory for males in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: All able-bodied men of the age of 18 had that obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And at the time that you completed your service in December of 1991, would you agree with me that within the JNA unit that you served in, there were not any tensions between the conscripts and officers of various ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to get your clarification of some of the people that were mentioned from Sanski Most. First of all, with respect to Danilusko Kajtez, am I correct that at the time that you encountered him in the woods on the 2nd of November 1992 when he and his cohorts did the crime that you have testified about, at that time you did not know this individual or his name; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: That is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that the first time that you heard the name of Danilusko Kajtez in relation to this incident was from Ms. Nada Ilicic at the hospital in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. I first heard of it from Mile Dosenovic, an inspector who came to see me in the hospital in Banja Luka on the 7th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did Ms. Nada Ilicic also mention the name of Danilusko Kajtez to you at some point in the hospital in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: She did not mention that name in hospital because -- I mean, she visited me only once up there, at the surgery department. She did not know of him at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And at the time of the incident in the woods this individual, Mr. Kajtez, he was the one dressed entirely in civilian clothes; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: That is accurate. But she had a submachine-gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just for clarifying the record, sir, the transcript reflects that you had referred to "she" having "a machine-gun." Are you talking about Danilusko Kajtez having the submachine-gun?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: It's not that I think so. I am saying that he did have one.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, am I correct that you have in some of your other statements detailed other crimes committed by this Danilusko Kajtez, including the killing of Mate Barac on the 18th of October 1992 at the request of a neighbour who wanted to steal the land of Mr. Barac?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with regard to this killing of Mr. Barac, this Danilusko Kajtez was given a payment by this private citizen, this neighbour who wanted to steal the land; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was given a reward of 10 metres of chopped wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that when talking about Kajtez, Danilusko Kajtez, we are talking about someone who is a common criminal used to doing things for his own financial gain?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: I cannot exactly agree with that. I mean, well, a criminal does not do such horrible things. A criminal does tend to hide that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now the other individuals that were with Danilusko Kajtez that participated in the crime in the forest, they were all known to you as fellow residents of Sanski Most; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to the persons who were killed or those who were there with him to kill others?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm asking about those individuals who were with Danilusko Kajtez and who participated in the crime of killing your neighbours and wounding you.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: I didn't know them. I mean, well, the inspector who came to see me in Banja Luka told me about that, and then all of these names were identified on the basis of the statement that I gave to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see that we're at the 10.31 mark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But before we take a break -- we'll take a break of 20 minutes. Witness, would you please follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Meanwhile, I put on the record the information which the Chamber now has received not yet in an official report but unofficially. The information being that when the transport police was ready to pick up Mr. Mladic at the UNDU at 8.30 this morning, that the transport police were informed by the United Nations Detention Unit Mr. Mladic is having breakfast at the moment and that he indicated he is not ready for transport yet. At 9.20 the transport police passed on the information that the UNDU security personnel were making attempts to make Mr. Mladic ready for transport but that Mr. Mladic was not showing any intention to make any hurry to get ready, and finally at 9.30 that the transport police gave information available to them that they had Mr. Mladic inside their vehicle, going to leave the UNDU to make their way towards the ICTY building. In addition to these reports, Mr. Mladic was informed once he had arrived at the ICTY premises, that he is welcome to enter the courtroom after the first break, and he was also offered by security to follow the proceedings from the holding cell where a monitor is placed until the first break takes place, and that Mr. Mladic has indicated that he does not want to follow the proceedings from the holding cell, but, rather, stay inside cell 10. That's the information which the Chamber has by now. We will take a break and we'll resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I put on the record that Mr. Mladic is present in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, if you are ready to proceed, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, I'd like to continue asking you now about the other individuals that assisted Mr. Kajtez in performing the crime, the execution. I'd like to focus for the time being on the one individual who was across the river by the sand-bed with a machine-gun. Am I correct that I am referring to Todor, Tode Vokic?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that his name was Tode Vokic. However, his real name is Todor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And this Todor, or Tode, Vokic, at the time of the incident he was a minor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would it also be correct that as a minor he would officially be too young to serve in the army?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: As far as serving in the army is concerned, yes, he was too young. But I don't know how come that he had a submachine-gun and was wearing a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to explore that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can call up in e-court document 1D385.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And while we wait for that, sir, I'd like to introduce for you that this is the statement given by yourself before the court in Sanski Most on the 8th of March, 1996. And I'd like to turn to page 2 in the B/C/S, and page 3 in the English, and I'd like to focus on the middle of the page in both versions. And the part in English begins: "There was also Todor Vokic..." And in the B/C/S it starts -- in B/C/S: [B/C/S spoken]. Sir, I think that there is a slight variance between the B/C/S original and the English translation of this section, so I would ask you to read for us the selection that begins at the part that I have just referenced and continues to describe this individual, Todor Vokic, and it's the first three sentences.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Can you mark the exact paragraph and can I have it enlarged, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the B/C/S it is right now located in the middle of the page. And the -- the -- the defining text is referencing Vokic, Mirka, and Dragica, Todor zvani [phoen] Tode.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: "Todor Vokic, aka Tode, son of Mirko and Dragica, was there as well. He was 4 to 5 metres away from us across the stream."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If you could continue, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness apparently has difficulties in reading it. Could it be enlarged so that it's easier for him to ... Are you able to read it, Mr. Stojic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But if it can be enlarged just a little bit more, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Has the witness only the B/C/S version on his screen? If not, then we should use that facility to enable him to better read. Yes. Is it better now, Mr. Stojic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is. Only ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You had read up to the point that he was at the other side of the stream. If you can find it ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. "... on a sandy patch. He was in charge and he would be the one who would commit the killings, or rather the shooting. He was a minor. He was also dressed in a Chetnik uniform and had insignia like the rest of them. He was standing on that sandy embankment, pointing submachine-gun towards the four men. When we were approaching this location where the crime would take place, when we were brought there, Niki, Zarko started shouting, My poor kids, and he started crying. However, the Chetniks showed no sympathy and Nikic, Pero was crying too."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now if we can focus back on this description that you gave of this described, Todor Vokic. Does this selection that you have read for us from your statement to the Sanski Most Court in March of 1996 accurately identify Todor Vokic as the main shooter or the one in charge?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: I cannot know exactly because I had my back turned to those who were shooting. Whether the others ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. Could you describe for us the type of weapon, or it's described here as either a light machine-gun or a submachine-gun. Could you clarify for us what type of weapon this individual, Todor Vokic, had in his possession?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: All four of them had submachine-guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were you familiar with the type of submachine-gun, based upon your time spent in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Are you able to identify the type of submachine-gun?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: The submachine-gun was the one on which I am forgetting at the moment how you pronounce it, but it's a rifle grenade. And it has a -- two legs that can be stretched, and a person shooting from it can do so whilst lying on the ground. There were no other types of submachine-guns at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that the submachine-guns that these individuals were carrying had some modifications to the butt of the rifle, some carvings?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: The insignia were etched; perhaps the four Ss, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me from your time spent in the JNA that it would not be normally permitted for soldiers to carve any kind of lettering into the butt of their issued rifle?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Well, you're now going back to regular service in the army and a state of war is a completely different thing. And it's been distributed in such a way that it can be carried on held in that manner. When people served in army as regular soldiers, it was not even allowed to take weapons outside of the army premises and people were held accountable for even one bullet missing or any other item missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And now you've described that this individual, Todor Vokic, the minor, had a camouflage uniform, a Chetnik uniform with the insignia, as you've described it. Could you describe for us, as best as you can, the particular Chetnik uniform that Todor Vokic was wearing that day, including any insignia or emblems?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No consultations in court. Little notes. Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic, Mr. Ivetic, no consultations in court, that's the regime. Little notes, if need be. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Perhaps it would assist if I repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, you've described that this individual, Todor Vokic, the minor, had a camouflage uniform, a Chetnik uniform with the insignia as you described it. Could you describe for us as best as you can the particular Chetnik uniform that Todor Vokic was wearing that day, including any insignia?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, it was not described. He had a camouflage uniform, he had no cap on the head, but the description was given of the other one who was dressed in military police uniform. He had a white belt, a submachine-gun, a pistol, handcuffs, and a cap on his head, with a cockade on it, and he was the one who searched us.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that only one of the individuals there in a camouflage uniform had the white belt and white pistol holster?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. And that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to now turn to 1D384. And when that document comes up I would be focussing on the first page in both languages in e-court. And, sir, for your information the document that is now coming up is a news article from the "Dnevni Avaz's" paper's crime section.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, before you continue, what do you want to do with the previous document or did you only want to use it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I might actually come back to it, but for the -- I thought -- I was only using it for that one section and so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have read that out to him and that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now we have this document before us - and I apologise, the B/C/S looks a little bit less clear than I remember it. But if we could focus on the -- first of all, this is an article from February of 1998 in the "Dnevni Avaz," sir. Looking at the caption or the title of this -- of this article, are you familiar with the article; that is to say, have you seen this article previously?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: There's a big lettering which says "Serbs kill nine Croats"; whereas the rest of it is invisible.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we look at the second full paragraph, and perhaps we can try to enlarge the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's going to be the second -- yeah, there we go. In that section. And it starts off the criminal charges -- we had it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you see there, sir, where it starts off with the criminal charges were filed, have been filed against Todor, Todo, father's name Mirko Vokic, born in Germany in 1977; Goran, father's name Radivoje Vukojevic, born in Prijedor in 1975; and Dane Danilusko, father's name Gojko Kajtez, born in Sanski Most in 1968. These men were resident in the Kruhari settlement during the entire occupation of Sanski Most. Criminal charges have also been filed against Milos, father's name Milorad, Maksimovic born in 1972 in Banja Luka where he has a permanent address. Now --

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And we've already previously discussed Mr. Todor, Tode, Vokic. Now we see that would have been 15 at the time of the incident. We also see that the individual Milos Maksimovic was born in 1972. That would make him 17 years old at the time of the shooting. Would you agree that Mr. Maksimovic at 17 years of age would have been too young to officially serve in the army, according to the conscription and mobilisation rules?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You say a person born in 1972 would have been 17 by 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It might be a different document. We'll get to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In any event, is this the same -- if we could focus on the Todor, Todo, Vokic, would this be the same person - they list a different nickname, "Todo" instead of "Tode" - is that your understanding to be the same individual that we talked about previously?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the same individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now if can I correctly focus on Goran Vukojevic, born in Prijedor in 1975, that would be the individual who was 17 at the time of the shooting and which I would ask you: Based upon him being 17 years of age, would you agree that he would be too young to serve officially in the army based upon the rules of conscription and mobilisation as you knew them in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's too young under regular circumstances and when a country is in a regular state. It is known that these people were minors.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We are not able to understand the answer. Can the witness please rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, the interpreters have interrupted that they did not understand and follow your answer. Could you please begin your answer from the beginning and give it in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Speaking of regular army, as the situation was when the country was in normal state, they were too young. However, this is not a regular army. We are talking here about criminals who were armed and were committing crimes at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Can we -- can we have this document introduced as the next available 1D exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before we do so. What's the year of this publication?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe it's 1998. If we scroll up to the original on the top there is an "8." I note that the English translation that was provided to us for this document does not appear to have the date, but if we focus there in the middle of the top of the page in the B/C/S, and if we can zoom in, I think we might be able to see it, although this copy is a lot less clearer than the copy I was working off of. So on the left-hand side if we can zoom on the top, after "Crna Hronika" or crime diary there's two lines that gives the date of this publication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I did this before and that's the reason I am asking you, because I fully understand those translated this to be unable -- I see a 1, a 9, another 9 but very vaguely, and what then follows is pretty unclear to me. If you further enlarge it --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It doesn't come clear on here. What I could do is I could at the next break have a paper version printed and I can do it off the copy that I had on the computer screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, any objections against?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: We have no objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And do you have -- do you agree with Mr. Ivetic that it should be 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I agree that the date is unclear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's a different kind of agreement than I had in my mind. But, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D384 becomes Exhibit D76, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence, but the Chamber would like to receive a better legible copy, and perhaps then even we could have a new translation on the basis of that new version.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will -- I will make sure that that is done, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, this article also mentions the filing of charges by the police of the Una-Sana canton of the federation of BiH after the war's end. Do you have knowledge of such criminal charges having actually been filed?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: I heard of that, but I learned about this from the press. Just like you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, for the record, the Una-Sana canton, that's within the federation of BiH, not within the Republika Srpska; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now if we can turn to Prosecution 65 ter number 19481, and should be a statement dated 10th of February 1993, which you gave to some authorities in BiH, and if my notes are accurate this one was not tendered by the Prosecution, so it should still be under the 65 ter number 19481. And once we get that document, I would be interested in page 5 in the English --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you repeated the number, it is recorded incorrectly, so that we have it clear on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. Thank you, Your Honour. Prosecution 65 ter number 19481. And the fifth page in English and the -- this will be a corresponding to the sixth page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, here I would direct your attention to the discussion where you mention a number and are recorded as saying "that you know exactly that a man by the name of Rade Kondic shot at you from behind." Do you see that part in this --

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it. And I said that I made a mistake when I mentioned his name. I was wrong about the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I apologise. When you said you had made a mistake, you mentioned his name. Was Rade Kondic not one of the individuals that was there?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you have a correction for who was there instead of Rade Kondic that this refers to?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Instead of him, Todor Vokic was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. That is what I had thought but wanted to make sure. Now, I think that we don't need this document. That's been cleared up sufficiently. Now, am I correct that you did not actually hear who it was that gave the command for the shooting to start in the forest on the date of the crime?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: I said that we had our backs turned. When we were lined up, we were actually shot at from the back. I don't know which one of the four issued the order. I just heard the command, "Start."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Would it be fair to say that either Danilusko Kajtez or Tomo -- Todor, Tode, Vokic appeared to be in charge for everything up to and leading up to the shooting, the parts that you did see?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: As for what I saw, I described that. I already described that, where this Todor Vokic stood opposite the stream. Then Danilusko Kajtez and those other two were searching us, just before the execution. And they beat us too and they took away our documents and everything that we had on us.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I appreciate that, sir. And based upon that description, I was asking -- did it appear that at the time that Danilusko Kajtez and/or Todor Vokic were in charge of and giving instructions to the men who searched you and beat you, the other two?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: We were beaten by this person who was dressed like a military policeman and this Danilusko. As for this other one, on the other side, he took the things that were being taken away from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let's focus then on this Danilusko. Did Danilusko Kajtez appear to be in charge of the events leading up to the shooting. I understand that you could not see the shooting, but everything that occurred previously, did it appear to you that Danilusko Kajtez was in charge?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: It's not that it appeared to me that way. I heard that from people who knew him and from Serbs who said that he left from Kruhari and that he was going up to Skrljevita to cleanse Glamocnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when you say "he," are we talking about Danilusko Kajtez, the one who was dressed in a civilian outfit?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just prior to when they opened up fire on you and your neighbours, they proclaimed that they were Seselj's army; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And after the shooting, all four of these individuals that had participated in the crime that were in the camouflage uniforms and the one that was in a civilian uniform that you have identified as the perpetrators, am I correct that they fled the scene of this crime?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And I'd like to return to 1D385, which we have looked at previously. This is again, sir, the report that you gave to the investigating judge Adil Draganovic of the Sanski Most Court on 8 March, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now I'd like to turn to page 3 in the B/C/S, and 3 in the English as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And perhaps the easiest way to locate the part that I'd like to focus on would be for me to read the English and allow you to then find that in the B/C/S, as it's -- it's typed rather busily on the paper. Perhaps even we could have the B/C/S up for the witness and zoomed in, and I will read the part that begins: "While I was lying down, I heard them say, Let's run. When they had run away, I lay still for another minute or two and I heard the clattering of weapons as they ran." Sir, have you and able to locate that portion of this statement?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: If can you enlarge it a bit. All right. "When they ran away, I remained there lying for another minute or two. I heard the rattling of weapons when they were running away, and I lifted my head, and I looked around to see whether they were still there somewhere nearby. Again, I laid down, and I got up again, and then I saw that they were no longer there. Then I got up and I saw a terrible sight."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Does this selection that first I started and then you read the remainder of it, does this accurately reflect your recollection of precisely what you saw immediately after you and the others were shot and also what you heard?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did it seem to you that these individuals, these perpetrators of this crime, were worried about being found out?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: I couldn't know it then that that is what they were worried about. Had they been worried, they wouldn't have done it in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would at this time tender this statement given by the witness before the Sanski Most court, dated 8th March 1996 as the next 1D exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Mr. Ivetic, for what purpose do you tender it? For the accuracy of the content or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No. Just for the sections that I've read. But in so far as -- as for completeness of the -- since the witness did correct the one section from previous where there was a word missing in the English so that we can have that all before us and we can understand the testimony that he has given. Not for the accuracy of the statement as a whole. Just the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But for the accuracy of the portions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Portions, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D385 becomes Exhibit D77, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Ivetic, I was asking you about this because it -- to have portions of a document which are there in translation, to have the translation corrected by reading out the English and then have it interpreted in court is not the way in which we should proceed. If there's any problem with a statement or a translation, then the translation should be verified. But interpreters do not have the task here to improve the translation of documents and then exactly if it is -- if then the document is admitted into evidence, then we have even two versions. The one in translation, the one as interpreted. And that's not what is in the standard work procedure for our interpreters and translators. Please be aware of that. And if you think that the translation needs to be corrected, then take care that it will.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would Your Honour, but this is a Prosecution document and therefore a Prosecution translation. My understanding is I'm not allowed to ask for re-translation of documents that CLSS has already translated for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not retranslation. But if you think there is an inaccuracy, then you can ask for a correction. That's a totally different matter. Everyone I take it, even the Prosecution, would appreciate that the accuracy of the translation is improved. Having dealt with the matter, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, am I correct that you later learned that when these individuals, these four killers, ran away, they encountered another individual, Karlo Tadic, an individual who knew them by sight, and that they killed him, too, in order not to be found out as having committed this crime?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What is right: That you heard this from other persons or that it happened? You're not an eye-witness to that, are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm not an eye-witness of that. But I heard later that they met him as they were going towards Sanski Most, that they came across him on the road, killed him, and threw him into the bushes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And do you know why they killed him? Were you told why they killed him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know why they killed him. They killed him because they were killing Croats that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ivetic, by this additional question it may be clear to you that putting such a composite question on what the witness may have heard is not the way to proceed. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then I'd like to call up 1D383, the statement given by the witness to the Zagreb authorities from ones I pooled this selection. And I also note that Karlo Tadic is one of the victims that the Prosecution has presented for this case and indeed was part of their direct examination with regard to this witness, so...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, I do not know what appears there, but you asked the witness whether they killed him because, and that's the only thing I commented on. That.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not that. Okay. We will see what we find in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 7 in the English and page 7 in the B/C/S, at the middle of the page in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, I'm focussing on the paragraph that begins: "Karlo Tadic was killed when the murderers returned to throw away the personal documents belonging to the executed people and when they saw that I was not there. They ran towards Sanski Most and near Stanoje Ninic's house, by the pear tree, they murdered Karlo, and threw his body into the bushes. They killed him simply because they had met him and were afraid that he would find out what they had done since he knew these people better than I did." And I'd like to ask you, sir, to verify: Is this entire account based upon what you heard after the event; that is to say, you did not actually eye-witness any of these portions?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. It is as it was described.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you have knowledge that Karlo Tadic knew these individuals or could recognise them?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have knowledge of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when you say have knowledge, would that be your personal knowledge or would that be something that you gained from third parties who told you that fact?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: No, this Karlo Tadic knew these people specifically. He went to work in that village before these unfortunate events and he moved around more than I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you one question, Witness. You earlier, when I asked you whether you knew why they killed Karlo Tadic, you said, Well, they were killing Croats on that day, and you do not know for any other reason. Now in the statement we find the specific reason is that they feared to be recognised by Karlo Tadic and that for that reason they killed him. Now, is it the one or the other? You see, the two answers, as far as the reasons for killing Karlo, are not entirely consistent. Could you explain to me and to my colleagues what is the true version?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This version, given in this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is, that they did not kill Karlo just because they were killing Croats but because they feared that he would -- he had recognised them and would tell what he had seen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could turn briefly to page 7 of this document in the English in e-court and page 7 also in the B/C/S. Oh, that's the same page, I guess. It's the next paragraph in the English and it should be the next paragraph in the B/C/S as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You are recorded here as saying, sir, and I will read the portion to you so you do not have to: "The most notorious Chetniks came from parts of Kruhari and Tramosnja, and the village of Susnjar. Everyone there was armed including women, children, and the elderly. They were all under arms." First of all, sir, do you stand by this selection from this statement as being -- as accurately reflecting your knowledge of these facts?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I stand by that. I stand by what I said already in that statement. Just one thing, it's not the village of Susnjar. It's a hamlet in Kruhari, close to Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that correction. And you identify then in this document individuals - specifically Nikola Jokic, Nedeljko Rasula, Vlado Vrkes, and Tomo Delis - as being the persons who were responsible for arming these individuals. First of all, I would like to ask you about Nikola Jokic, Nedeljko Rasula, Vlado Krkes. Am I correct that these were all civilians?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: This gentleman is not Krkes. It is Vrkes. Vlado Vrkes. I mean, I don't know whether they were civilians. As for this Bono who was killed, I heard that Tomo Delic was in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We'll get to Mr. Delic. I was focussing on these three individuals. Are you finished answering as to these three individuals, Mr. Vlado Vrkes, Nikola Jokic, and Nedeljko Rasula?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Nedeljko Rasula was the president of the municipal council in Sanski Most. So he was the mayor. Now whether he was in uniform or not, I mean, well, that I don't know. I did know that he went to the church in Sasina. He and other delegations. He went there to look for weapons, whether there were any in the church. I heard that from Vlado Tomic, the priest. That happened after Croats were killed in the village of Brisevo towards the end of July, the 26th, the 27th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And I'd like to now focus on the individual you've identified as Tomo Delic. Previously today you identified him as being the commander of the Serb armed forces in -- in Sanski Most. Am I correct that we are talking about the SOS?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that the SOS was a private military; that is to say, not the regular army, the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Private army, could be. But I don't know who you mean by regular army. Because when the Republika Srpska was formed -- I mean, are you referring to Republika Srpska or Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Either, or. Am I correct that the SOS was a separate formation from either the JNA or the VRS?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: It was separate from the JNA, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I put it to that you it was separate from VRS as well. Do you agree or disagree, or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: I would not agree with that. I would not agree that that is the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. If we can now focus on the months prior to the incident where you were wounded and your neighbours were killed, during that time-period, you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, before we enter a new subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We usually take the break after one hour. So, therefore, this would be the appropriate time for a break. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. Could you please follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I'd like to hear from you where we are as far as timing is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I should be able to finish, I think, within the next half-hour to 40 minutes, so in the next session I will be finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll take a break and we resume at a quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Perhaps we could use the time. There was an issue, Mr. Ivetic, the video which was MFI'd under number D43. There have been long discussions about the video, and I think that the latest was that the parties seemed to agree that the soundtrack of the video was a fabrication, and the Chamber wondered whether you still, under these circumstances, intend to tender D43?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe it's not necessary to tender it under that circumstances, although it was already tendered and it received a number. So I don't know if -- what the procedure would be to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It was MFI'd. Then we would not be asking for that to be entered as an exhibit based upon the subsequent information that we learned that the audio track was not the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's hereby on the record. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to remind the Chamber of the Prosecution's position that we -- the Prosecution believes it's important for the Chamber to still have access to that be -- in the event that other evidence from this particular web site is tendered so that the Chamber may properly evaluate it. We are happy for it to remained MFI'd wouldn't want it removed from the evidence in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the Chamber even asked for the matter to be investigated further, which -- therefore it's not done. It's just the procedural position of the Defence at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apologies, Mr. Stojic, for dealing with other matters when you entered the courtroom. Mr. Ivetic will now continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to focus on the time-period leading up to the incident in the woods, the killings, that you survived. Am I correct that in the time-period leading up to the 2nd of November, 1992, that there were no military operations by the army in your home village or the area where the crime took place?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And at the time of the murder, there were no tanks or military vehicles to be seen anywhere near the area where you survived the attempted killing.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, in fact, these criminals that shot at you and killed your neighbours in the woods, they never expressed or said that they were taking part in any planned activities of the army of the Republika Srpska; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: I don't know if they said that or not, but when they shot us, they told us that they were Seselj's army.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. When the -- strike that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can look at Prosecution 65 ter number 06374.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And while we wait for that document, sir, this is the report of the investigation performed by the investigative judge of the Sanski Most lower court, and it is dated the 3rd of November, 1992. Would you agree with me that it would seem that the authorities in Sanski Most undertook to investigate this crime the very next day after it occurred?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: That's what it says here in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. And in fact, you had spoken with the police from Sanski Most and told them what had happened when they directed you to the hospital for further treatment; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, the report is dated the 9th of November, and deals with, I think, an investigation which took place on the 3rd of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, I misspoke, Your Honours. I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can look at Prosecution 65 ter number 07050. And the B/C/S is a little bit faint, but I believe the date can be seen, and it would appear to be the 7th of December, 1992, a little over one month after the incident in question when the Banja Luka Military Court ordered that the suspects Danilusko Kajtez and Milos Maksimovic be detained into custody for this murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that only -- it is possible that only these two individuals were listed because the military court only had jurisdiction over these two rather than the two others who were minors?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot interpret whether that's the case or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was perhaps part of what you wanted to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, I was going [Overlapping speakers] ... so the witness can answer this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. But the witness has answered the question. This resolves the issue you wanted to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can call up Prosecution 65 ter number 06375 in e-court, the first page in both the B/C/S and the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
