utterances.text: And this document, sir, is dated the 7th of December, 1992, just over one month after the -- the -- the crime. And it is a report submitted by the military police company of the 6th Krajina Brigade of the VRS, and you will note here it lists the four persons responsible for the killing, including their dates of birth. Would you agree with me that the Tode Bokic who is listed there has the same father's name and the same date of birth as Tode Vokic whom we previously identified as the 15-year-old involved in the shooting?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this document details or mentions that an on-site investigation was conducted, that the weapons were seized, and an analysis of the weapons and empty cartridges was made. Would you agree with me that this would be the procedure you would expect for a legitimate investigation?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. That's how it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And this document says that all of the above persons were apprehended and processed. Would you agree with me that that would be the procedure that you would expect from a legitimate investigation.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: When investigation was ordered, then a proper procedure is only to be expected to be conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. If we can return to the "Dnevni Avaz" news article that is now Exhibit D76, and if we could focus on the first page in e-court. And when this comes up, if we can look at the bottom of the page in the English and the bottom of the first column in the B/C/S. And, sir, I will read out for so you do not have to, but you can locate then the text in the B/C/S. I want to focus on the part that begins as and reads as follows: "On the fatal day, Goran Vukojevic and Dane Kajtez Danilusko, armed with machine-guns, went to the house of Todor, Todo, Vokic with whom they had allegedly arranged to ambush and kill Croats of the Skrljevita village and thus avenge their friends who had been killed in [sic] the battle-field. Vokic accepted the plan." And then it continues. Is it correct, sir, that this is precisely the information that has come out in the investigation of the MUP of the Federation of BiH into this since; namely, that Kajtez and the 17-year-old Vukojevic agreed with the 15-year-old Vokic to ambush and kill some Croats to avenge the deaths of their friends in the battle-field?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: I heard that it was exactly as you described it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to turn to Prosecution 65 ter number 07074. This has been, I believe, marked as Exhibit P369. And it will be page 1 in both languages that we need to look at first.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, for the first question I'd like to ask you about this document is the date. Would you agree with me that the date is the 2nd of June, 1993, and that this indictment was issued by the military prosecutors of the Republika Srpska less than eight months after the crime in question?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: That's what the document that I have in front of me says.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can now turn to the second page in both languages. There is a list of proposals on that page. And I would direct for the time being to focus on number 7, which is a proposal to find these men guilty of the crime and to sentence them to the appropriate legal sanction and to base the same on the law. If we look at -- first of all, would you agree with me that that would be -- that it would appear that the military prosecutors are, in fact, condemning the crime, not condoning the crime?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: That's what the document reads.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, the witness has now several times answered the question by saying, That's what the document reads. He apparently is not familiar with the document. You're asking him to draw conclusions from what is found in the document. Apparently you consider this relevant information for the Chamber, which I can fully understand. Why not agree with the Prosecution that this document was produced at the time that this happened. Apart from how it then continued, whether this was the end of the story or not. But the cause of death was examined on the spot, the witness seems to have no specific knowledge about that. I mean, these kind of documentary evidence, why not agree on this is the steps that were taken at the time, were recorded, and then where it stops or where it doesn't stop we'll then -- perhaps there it becomes interesting as well. Why is there any problem with that, Mr. Jeremy? To say, Well, this was an indictment that was brought against these persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a document that I've tendered as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So why ask the witness what the prosecution, at the time here by doing this, may have thought? Does the witness know anything about who the prosecutor was, what he had on his mind? What we know is the documents that were created at the time and seem to indicate that the prosecution at least was started, was initiated. I mean, I'm asking myself - and perhaps my colleagues as well - why ask the witness about all this?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, it highlights that the documentation presented by the Prosecution does not support their summary of the events in question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that's a discussion with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Agreed. But I'm also -- and trying to see with the witness. The part I would like to ask him now is the description of the crime --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. But let's -- if it doesn't support the case of the Prosecution, that's a matter for argument because this is what the document -- what the Prosecution itself puts forward as well. So apparently what does exists is a difference of interpretation on what these documents mean. Now, the witness cannot tell us anything about it. I mean, I only intervened after he had said a couple of times well, that's what the document says. Let's try to -- let's try to come to the core of what keeps the parties apart rather than to present highlighting portions to the witness who doesn't know anything about it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we can look at the first paragraph under the statement of reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And here, again, it is reported that the first and second accused were intending, allegedly, to take revenge for their friends killed in combat against Croatian and Muslim paramilitary formations in the war, and so they decided to waylay the inhabitants of the village of Skrljevita near the village of Glamocnica. Is it your understanding that this is what came out also now in the investigation conducted by the authorities of Republika Srpska into the crime that you were a victim of?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, you have just said - and it is true - that this is the first that I'm seeing these documents. And it is true that these documents truthfully describe what happened on the 2nd November 1992. However, this is the first time that I'm seeing these documents in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, your last question to the witness -- I invited you to proceed but it seems that you proceeded more or less ignoring what I said to you before. Isn't it? Because to ask the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: He was a witness in that case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- is this your understanding of what also came out also in the investigation conducted -- what we see here, this is reported as the outcome of the investigation conducted by the authorities. What -- what -- if the witness has any specific knowledge whether it really reflects what they had on their minds, then, of course, it would make sense to ask him. But what is there which -- you're more or less asking whether this is what is reported as the result, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this witness was a witness in these proceedings before the authorities on this indictment. He was a witness. He testified. There was a judgement -- in fact, two judgements based upon this witness's testimony and testimony of others relating to the Scheduled Incident from the indictment, which I'm going into, which I'm asking about. I believe they're relevant. I believe they demonstrate that the charges cannot be related to my client and I'm entitled to ask them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But this witness, if you ask him, Is this the result of the investigations, if this is a report describing apparently the result of the investigations. And if the witness doesn't know anything about the investigations, then just agree with the Prosecution that this was reported at the time. We can then read what was reported and whether it supports your case or whether it supports the Prosecution's case is then a matter for argument. But I do not see how this witness can assist us in this respect. I'm not saying that witness is unable to testify about the events or about these proceedings, but here apparently the witness cannot assist us and that's what I tried to bring to your attention and which I now, again, tried to bring to your attention. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, is it true that the authorities of Republika Srpska actually held a trial against Danilusko Kajtez now known by his new name, Nikola Kovacevic, who was arrested, and also against Milos Maksimovic, who was arrested, in 2007?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any dispute about this, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It was not disclosed to me by the Prosecution, Your Honours, so I believe there might be.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'm not aware of this trial at this stage, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're not aware of the trial held against Danilusko Kajtez. Then there's no agreement on that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Stojic. Am I correct, sir, that the authorities of Republika Srpska, the courts held a trial against Danilusko Kajtez, now known by his new name Nikola Kovacevic, and against Milos Maksimovic in 2007?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: As I already said, according to the documents in front of me, one can read that. But I personally didn't have any knowledge about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the sake of the record, I think you referred to the year 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Page 54, line 2, at the end it should read 2007 instead. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I missed that in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, am I correct that you actually testified in the trial before the district court in Banja Luka in 2007 in the case against Mr. Danilusko Kajtez, now known as Nikola Kovacevic, and Mr. Milos Maksimovic?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is it also correct that other representatives of the other named victims also testified as part of these trial proceedings against Danilusko Kajtez, now known as Nikola Kovacevic, and Milos Maksimovic in 2007?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Who are you referring to when you say "the other".

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: For instance Nevenka Tutic?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe also Nada Ilicic.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Nada Ilicic? That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Perhaps it's not that relevant. I'd like to focus on your testimony during that trial. Is it correct, as it is record in the judgement of that case, that you were unable to identify Danilusko Kajtez, now known Nikola Kovacevic, as one of the persons who perpetrated the crime against you?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is it also correct that you are unable to identify Milos Maksimovic, the other accused, as having been one of the perpetrators in the crime that was committed against you?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you know that on the 13th of December, 2007, the district court in Banja Luka acquitted both defendants?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I saw that on Croatian TV, Nova. And it wasn't the basic court in Banja Luka. It was the district court in Banja Luka. And it said -- I mean, they described it -- these crimes correctly, and the district court of Banja Luka set them free. When they went out to take their revenge against the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you know that on 19 June 2008 the Supreme Court affirmed this acquittal judgement of these two persons?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear of this, before this Honourable Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you for clearing that up. Now I'd like to go over some points --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, may I interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to put one question in relation to the last matter. Sir, can you help me: How was it you were asked to identify these two people? How were you supposed to identify them in that court proceedings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what they asked for. They asked me to identify their faces or their voices. That is how they asked me to identify them. When this crime took place, it was a matter of seconds, because that moment, had I known them, I would have said during the first investigation in Sanski Most what their names were. I would not have identified them -- I mean, the investigation that went on, that continued, showed that these were the persons that I had described, to the best of my recollection. Before this court, I testified just like here. I said whatever it was that I had to say. The only thing was that I recognised their faces, their voices, whether I can remember that, whether I can remember their voices, at that moment when they were searching us and mistreating us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Were you asked to identify their faces and voices during the proceedings in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did you have seen these two people before in the time before the -- the events you testified about and where you were injured? In the time between the murder operation and the -- and the court proceedings, did you see these two people at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, I only saw them on the day when I suffered so much. When they wanted to execute us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'd now like to briefly cover some points relating to your testimony in relation to the time-period that you spent in the hospital in Banja Luka. Am I correct that the soldier guarding your room in the hospital kept the doorknob to your door on his person; that is to say, in his pocket?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. He kept it. I don't know whether he kept it in his pocket though.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that this would seem to indicate his job was to keep people out of your room rather than to keep you in your room?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Well, that should have been his job. However, unfortunately, different things happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can we also agree that the guard, or guards, who let people in to mistreat you were therefore not properly doing their job to protect you from such abuse?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: That's right. If their job was to protect us, then they shouldn't have been allowed in without his approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And isn't it correct that while you were being transported from the medical centre in Sanski Most to the hospital in Banja Luka, that a policeman was escorting you in the ambulance, and you were told that this was for your safety, to keep you safe from extremists?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in the ambulance you were not mistreated.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can also talk about the soldiers that you said used to come in and beat you in the hospital, if we can -- if I can ask you this: In the Brdjanin trial, at transcript page 6789, lines 13 through 12 [sic], that would be page 29 in e-court of P365, I will read for you, sir, what you said there because we do not have the transcript in B/C/S. And please follow along. "Q. Who did the beating? "A. We were beaten by civilians and by soldiers and by anyone who could enter that cell. "Q. And when you are referring to soldiers, can you be more specific? What kind of soldiers? "A. Serbian soldiers. "Q. Can you even be more specific. Were they regular, reservist, military police? "A. Who knows what they were like. I think they were the ones who were sent away, who weren't under control. They were out of control." Does -- do you agree with me that --

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not understand what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please finish your question. And could you please carefully listen to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: My question for you, sir: Does this selection that I've just read for you, does it comport with your recollection and your impression as to these soldiers that would come in to mistreat you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm told maybe there was not a translation of the question so perhaps I could repeat it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please then repeat the whole of the question, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: My question is as follows, sir: Does this selection that I've just read to you, does it comport with your recollection and your impression as to these soldiers that would come in to mistreat you?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the hospital in Banja Luka, was it a civilian institution or a military hospital?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: It was a civilian hospital. The clinical centre in the very centre of the town of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, for clarifying that. During the total time-period that you were at the hospital, am I correct that you were only exposed to physical harassment or beating on a total of two occasions?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: That's what I stated and that is how I remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And how long was your stay in the hospital, sir, if you -- if you can give us an indication?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: 32 days in a cell. Nine days all together. I mean, 39 days all together. But out of the 39, 32 in a cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that clarification, sir. Now, in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry for interrupting you, but I'm now a little bit confused. Please clarify for me. I understood you were in a civilian hospital. Was there a cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. I said cell, number 8. And number 9. That's what was established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes. But were you locked up in the cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'd also like to -- was this a real cell or was it a room which was locked which you couldn't leave; or was it really like - I don't know to what extent you are familiar with what a prison cell looks like, but that means very heavy locks and usually a small window and a door - was that the situation, or was it a room locked and with not much furniture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a hospital room that was turned into a prison, into a cell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was there a window in that room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were there bars before the window?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. But, after all, it is a hospital, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You would say you were staying in a room. Was it a small room or a large room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it wasn't a large room. There were four beds there, and I was lying in one of these beds. And next to me this gentleman who was a victim of Manjaca; he had no legs. And in those two other beds there were two other men. There was another man with an amputated leg; and in yet another bed, there were two Bosniaks in that one bed. So the total was five. There were five of us there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you couldn't leave that room because the handle was not available to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right. And we were guarded there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. How did doctors enter that room and leave that room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, it was the soldier who would let them in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the doctors themselves could not open the door to come in or to leave the room you were in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, they couldn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The -- during the time-period that you were at the hospital, the two occasions that you identify when you were physically mistreated, were they on the same day or were they on two separate days out of the 39?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: On two separate days.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct on one of the occasions it was an inebriated soldier?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And am I correct that on -- on the other occasion it was not a soldier but was a member of the hospital staff?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Not a member of the hospital staff. It was a soldier, too, the person who beat me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can ask you one more question in relation to the entire time-period when the individuals who you have described as Danilusko Kajtez and the other three individuals who were in camouflage uniforms, during the incident in the forest where they took aside, mistreated you, and then killed your colleagues and attempted to kill you, at no time did Mr. Kajtez or any of his cohorts ever mention the names of General Talic, General Mladic, or Radovan Karadzic, did they?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: That's right. They asked about people from my area.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to again express sympathy for myself and my client for all you have endured. I thank you for helping us to illuminate this matter today and I have no further questions for you at this time.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Ivetic, just to clarify, the documents you used, you do not intend to tender them. You used 65 ter 19481, which is the BiH witness statement, 10th of February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe I only -- I used one selection from that document, and it's a document that I think seven pages in total. So I would -- I wasn't going to tender it. The one paragraph that we read into it was the extent of what I wanted to focus the witness, but if Your Honours would like to [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just wanted to have everything clear that what you used. If you do not tender it we just stick to the portion you read. The same would be true for the statement of the witness given on the 20th of January, 1994, to the centre for collection of documents and processing of data on the homeland war, 1D00383.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That is correct. In so far as the witness identified the error in personam of the individual and that's been clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the report by Dr. Prosic [phoen] on the nine persons that were killed in the forest.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't know that the witness can authenticate a report or provide any additional information about that, so that was why I didn't tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. 07050, ruling of the Banja Luka military court investigating judge and -- finding that two accused, including Danilusko Kajtez should be detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct. And again, that would be something that the witness would not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just -- you don't to explain. And the same would be true then for 06375, a report from Prejdag [phoen] Lasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Jeremy, any need to put further questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes I have a few questions in re-direct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, at temporary transcript page 11, line 16, you state that a Mrs. Nada visited you on 9 November and helped you to be released from hospital. Firstly, is the date 9 November the correct date?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: No. On the 11th. I mean, on the 11th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojic. In addition, in connection with this release, at temporary page 11, line 19 of the transcript, you describe Mrs. Nada having lunch with "them." Who were you referring to by "them"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't recall this arising out of the cross-examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a clarification to the transcript. My recollection is that the witness at the time named who he had lunch with and I'd like to make that clarification now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If -- so you're seeking to clarify the transcript which you --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, would you please repeat the question and then the witness may answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, in connection with your release from hospital, at temporary page 11, line 19, you described Mrs. Nada having lunch with "them." Who were you referring to by "them"?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: What I meant was when she went to the military command in order to get approval to set me free, she said that she had lunch at the military command. They offered lunch and she did have lunch there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojic. Mr. Stojic, at temporary transcript page 58 and 59, you were asked about soldiers who beat you in your cell in Banja Luka hospital. Specifically you referred to those who were sent away. Were these the same soldiers who were guarding your cell in Banja Luka hospital?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: What do you mean? Who are you referring to? Sent away, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Defence counsel quoted a section of your testimony in the Brdjanin case where you referred to being beaten by soldiers who were sent away. Were these soldiers who were sent away - to use your words - the same soldiers who were guarding your cell in Banja Luka hospital?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I meant them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So when you referred to being beaten by an inebriated soldier, was this the soldier who was guarding your cell?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't the one who was on guard. It was one from the street who was let in.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And who let this man in to your cell?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: The guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, you'll recall at temporary transcript page 21, line 12 to 14, Mr. Ivetic stated: "When talking about Kajtez, Danilusko Kajtez, we can talk about someone who was a common criminal, who used to do things for his own financial gain."

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honour, while I don't propose to ask the witness questions about Mr. Kajtez's military affiliation, I would simply like to point out for the record that a number of the documents from the Banja Luka military court, for example --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there -- if you're drawing our attention to that, does the witness need to hear that at this moment? You were about, I take it, to ask a question, and that's something different from addressing the Court and pointing out certain matters. You can do that perhaps after the witness has answered your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I can do that if you would prefer, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: There wasn't a follow-up question to the witness. I simply wanted to make an observation relevant to this question for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But once the witness is here -- I mean, you're still examining him, then to address the Court and draw our attention to matters may draw the attention of the witness to certain matters as well and that's, of course, not what we're trying to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: That's understood, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: On that basis, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, have the questions in re-examination triggered any need for further questions on your part.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Stojic, this concludes your evidence in this court. I'd like to thank you very much for travelling along way to The Hague and for answering all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Judges, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, of course, I wouldn't know what at this moment you would like to bring to the attention of the Chamber and whether it's appropriately done at this moment or whether you leave it for later when argument is -- really starts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: It's just a very short observation that I would like to make at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: It is simply there were questions put to the witness about Mr. Kajtez's being a common criminal, and I simply wanted to point out that contained within exhibits before this Court tendered through this witness from the Banja Luka military court are details about the affiliation that Danilusko Kajtez and Milos Maksimovic had to the 6th Krajina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, in full fairness, Mr. Ivetic, if you would like to address as matter as well without going into full argument then, of course, you have an opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The documents do indicate that soldiers in their personal time engaged in personal events that were considered a crime by the prosecutors of that same army that they were -- that an indictment was issued with respect to the crimes committed by these individuals who will -- were affiliated with the 5th or 6th, I forget, there was one mentioned, it was 6th Krajina Brigade, in the documents. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I think it is time to take a break. After the break, the Chamber would like to deliver a few decisions also relevant in relation to the next witness, although not exclusively, which will take some -- I think up to some 12 minutes. And would the Prosecution then be ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll resume at 25 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As I said before the break, I'd like to deliver a few decisions. The first one is a decision on the Prosecution motion to admit exhibits associated with Rule 92 ter statements of Witness RM-066 and guidance related to that matter. It's a decision with regard to the Prosecution motion to admit into evidence five documents associated with the witness statement of Witness RM-066 and will provide additional guidance to the parties on the admissibility of documents used with witnesses. On the 17th of September, 2012, the Prosecution sought to tender into evidence five documents associated with the statement of Witness RM-066. The Defence objected to the documents' admission on the grounds that Witness RM-066 did not have a sufficient personal basis of knowledge about them and was not a "good source" to confirm their authenticity. The Chamber marked these documents for identification as P186, P188, P189, P190, and P192. On the 17th of September, 2012, the Defence elaborated on its objections to which the Prosecution responded on the 18th of September. On the 19th of September, the Prosecution provided the Chamber with additional information on the provenance of the documents. The Defence submits that it is improper for these five documents to be admitted through Witness RM-066 because the witness does not have sufficient personal knowledge to meet the foundational requirements for such admission. The Defence submits that the Chamber's evidentiary standard has been that unless a witness can demonstrate personal knowledge or experience regarding the entirety of a document, the document should not be admitted through that witness and only the witness's testimony about the limited part of the document upon which he has knowledge should form part of the record. The Prosecution submits that the parties may seek to tender into evidence documents which have been discussed by the witness in the statement or in previous testimony, and that any document which forms an inseparable and indispensable part of the witness's written evidence may be admitted into evidence. The Prosecution submits that this test for admissibility is met if the witness discusses the document or if the written statement or transcript would have less probative value without the admission of the document. The Chamber will now clarify the standard for the admission of documents through witnesses. The Chamber generally prefers that a witness, through whom a document is tendered, has personal knowledge about the document. However, the Chamber clarifies that a document's probative value may also be established by having a witness testify about events described in a certain document. If the content of a document used during a witness's examination is sufficiently linked to the content of that witness's testimony, the document may be appropriately tendered and admitted with that witness, even if the witness is unfamiliar with the specific document. This standard is also in line with the Chamber's previous guidance where it indicated a preference for documentary evidence to be tendered in court with witnesses, rather than from the bar table. In light of this additional guidance, the Chamber hereby admits MFI'd documents P186, P188, P189, P190, and P192 into evidence. The Prosecution also tendered 65 ter number 6931 as a closely related document to P189. This document is also admitted into evidence, but we still need a number for that. Madam Registrar, 65 ter number 6931 would receive number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number P377, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P377 is admitted into evidence. Finally, document P201 was MFI'd due to very similar circumstances during the testimony of Witness Vulliamy. In light of the Chamber's additional guidance, this document is also admitted into evidence. And this concludes the Chamber's discussion. Now, in relation to a similar issue which arose today, that is in relation to P366, marked for identification, for the same reasons as given for the other documents in the decision I delivered on behalf of the Chamber, P366 is admitted into evidence. The Chamber rejects the position taken by the Defence that statements taken and to be used in evidence for the truth of their contents should always be under 92 bis, 92 ter, or 92 quater. If they're not taken for the purposes of the proceedings of this Tribunal, the case law does not applies [sic] such a strict test. Further, the handwritten letter, because that's what we are talking about, Mr. Ivetic, one of the documents you tendered and which was admitted into evidence, which is a newspaper article, which, of course, the witness didn't have any specific knowledge about the newspaper article, even refers to that same letter, and that would be a far more indirect way of bringing this letter to the attention of the Chamber than to have the letter itself admitted into evidence. P366 is, therefore, admitted into evidence. Then more directly linked to the next witness, I would now like to deliver the Chamber's decision with regard to the Defence notice objection and motion to bar witness Dorothea Hanson from testifying as an expert, a motion which was filed on the 15th of October, 2012. The Prosecution responded on the 22nd of October, and the Chamber will also decide on the Prosecution's request to add a number of documents referred to in the Hanson report to its Rule 92 ter exhibit list. The request was made in the Prosecution notice of disclosure of the Hanson report which was filed on the 17th of September 2012. The Defence has not responded to this request. As for the applicable law concerning expert evidence and additions to the Rule 65 ter exhibit list, the Chamber refers to its decision concerning Richard Butler, a decision of the 19th of October 2012, and its decision on the Prosecution second motion to amend Rule 65 ter exhibit list, a decision delivered on the 27th of June, 2012. Finally with regard to the Defence requests to cross-examine the witness, the Chamber notes that the witness will be called to testify and the Defence will therefore have the opportunity to cross-examine her. Based on the foregoing, the Chamber decides that witness Hanson may testify as an expert witness and denies the Defence request to bar the Prosecution from presenting her evidence. The Chamber defers its decision on admission of the Hanson report until the time of the witness's testimony. With regard to the addition of 39 documents to the Prosecution's Rule 65 ter exhibit list, the Chamber considers that the documents are prima facie relevant and of probative value and that the Prosecution has provided good cause as to why these documents were not added prior to the finalisation of the Hanson report. The Chamber notes that the Defence did not respond to the request and did therefore not make any submissions as to whether the addition would cause any burden on them. The Chamber further considers that most of the documents are only one or two pages long. And based on the forgoing, the Chamber finds that it is in the interests of justice to add the documents to the Prosecution's exhibit list. The Chamber therefore grants the Prosecution's request. That concludes the Chamber's decision on this matter. The third and last one ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have to re-read the -- at least parts of the recent decision. Apparently it takes some effort to be back in court after not having been in court for two days. I missed the back part of this decision. I referred to the applicable law concerning expert evidence and additions to the Rule 65 ter list and that the Chamber refers to its decision concerning Richard Butler, a decision of the 19th of October, and a decision on the Prosecution second motion to amend Rule 65 ter exhibit list, a decision of the 27th of June 2012. The Defence has argued in this context that Witness Hanson is not an expert and should therefore not be allowed to present expert evidence before the Chamber. The witness's CV and the submissions by the Prosecution indicate that the witness has completed advanced studies and has extensive working experience in the field of modern Balkan history. In particular, the witness has worked as a research officer at the Office of the Prosecutor for the past 13 years, where she has studied Bosnian Serb institutions, including Crisis Staffs. On this basis, the Chamber is satisfied that the witness is a historical expert who can assist the Chamber on matters related to Crisis Staffs, War Presidencies, and war commissions in the Bosnian Serb Republic during 1991 to 1995. The Defence further argues that, and I quote, "it cannot be excluded that Ms. Hanson personally, as well as professionally, is a potentially biased participant in this case," and that's the end of the quote. The only basis for this assertion is the witness's employment with the Office of the Prosecutor. In this respect, the Chamber refers to its decision on the matter of bias in the decision concerning Richard Butler of the 19th of October, 2012; paragraph 16. The Chamber finds the Defence`s allegation of bias to be unsubstantiated. As for any arguments related to the methodology, drafting, and content of the Hanson report, the Chamber considers that these are matters that can be and should be addressed during the examination of the witness. And then I continued with the portion I read already: "Finally, with regard to the Defence requests to cross-examine the witness, the Chamber notes that the witness will be called to testify and the Defence will therefore have the opportunity to cross-examine her." And what remains of the decision that Ms. Hanson may testify and also in relation to the 39 documents, the Prosecution wishes to add to its Rule 65 ter exhibit list, that part of the decision has been read already. Then I now move to the third decision I wanted to deliver. It is a decision and guidance on tendering of material underlying proposed expert reports. On the 10th of October, 2012, the Prosecution requested to be permitted to file an early bar table motion in relation to underlying documents of proposed expert reports. The Defence did not respond to this request. The Chamber will provide the parties with some further guidance in relation to this matter. Material underlying proposed expert reports should be accessible to all parties and may be used in court when examining the proposed expert witness. However, as a general rule, the Chamber expects the calling party not to tender such material just because a proposed expert referred to or used that document in compiling his or her report. If the Chamber determines a witness to be an expert, it requires full transparency of the facts the expert relied upon and of the methods used to form opinions and conclusions but does not require and will generally not accept that all this material is tendered. A proposed expert report should be clear enough in relation to describing and drawing conclusions from the underlying documents, so as to make the additional tendering of certain source and underlying material unnecessary. Notwithstanding this, the cross-examining party may tender certain materials when challenging the conclusions of the witness on the basis of the underlying documents. The Chamber itself may also wish to have certain documents in evidence. Furthermore, once a proposed expert witness's conclusions are challenged by the cross-examining party, the Chamber will also allow the calling party to tender certain underlying materials. As a result, the Prosecution should not file an early bar table motion in relation to underlying material of proposed experts. And the Chamber hereby denies the request. And this concludes the Chamber's decision and further guidance. Is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness, as I understand, Ms. Hanson.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Hanson.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You will first be examined by Ms. Bibles. You certainly are aware that Ms. Bibles is counsel for the Prosecution in this case. We have only a limited time left for today but we'll continue tomorrow. Ms. Bibles, if you're ready, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Can I first ask you to state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Dorothea Curtis Hanson.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask the Court Officer to call up 65 ter 11219, Ms. Hanson's curriculum vitae.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: While we're pulling this up, I'll ask if this is a copy of your CV that was prepared in 2008.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it appears to be.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And have you continued since 2008 to work in the OTP Leadership Research Team as a research officer?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And as you look at the documents in front of you, are there any changes or additions that you make to these documents today?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender 65 ter 11219.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not know from whom I expect whether there is any objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Miodrag Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 11219 becomes Exhibit P378, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Did you prepare a report in this case?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And can you describe for us how it relates to the report that you prepared in the case of Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: It is essentially the same report with just a few very minor corrections that I had noted in -- in my testimony at the time that needed correcting.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask the Court Officer to call up the first page of 65 ter 28454.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Could you look at the first page of this document and tell us if this is the report that you prepared in this case.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, it appears to be.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Are there any changes or corrections that you would make at this time to the report that's prepared in front of us?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: It's not a change. It is just one explanation I would like to make, if I might, in paragraph 10. And under taskings and methodology.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I believe that's page 3 in e-court. I believe... yes.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yeah, it's just the last two sentences there obviously apply to the Karadzic report, whereas it incorporates new evidence and a new section; that is, applies to the Karadzic report. The Mladic report does not differ from the Karadzic report, so that's -- the sentences perhaps are slightly misleading here. That's all I wanted to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you briefly summarise for us how this particular report was developed.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Well, many years ago now, at the time of the preparation of the Krajisnik case, I was tasked to research and explain to the Prosecution what were the structures and functions of Bosnian Serb Crisis Staffs. Out of my original research report, the Prosecution team decided to use it as an expert report so it became an expert report for Krajisnik. I continued working on it, updating it with new research, and a later -- another version was used when I testified based on this report for Stanisic Zupljanin -- or in the Stanisic Zupljanin case in the case against Gojko Klickovic at the Bosnian Serb state court -- I mean the Bosnian state court. I'm used to saying Bosnian Serbs all the time. The Bosnian state court in Sarajevo and then in the Karadzic case.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: In preparing --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: In preparing this report, could you tell us how you determined which materials to rely on in drawing your opinions?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Well, as I say, my original tasking was Bosnian Serb Crisis Staffs, so I had at my disposal various kinds of documents in the possession of the OTP. In some cases, entire collections of Crisis Staff minutes. In some cases, scattered examples of Crisis Staff decisions or minutes. In other cases, municipal gazettes. Some contemporary press I also looked at. And then just various documents collected by the OTP relating to Crisis Staffs. Obviously, the complete sets of minutes were the most useful, but in order to get as geographically and chronologically broad account I also -- I cast my net as wide as I could.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And could you tell us whether you worked with original documents or with translations.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: I worked with original documents preferably.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And just to clarify, you do read and understand B/C/S language and the Cyrillic alphabet?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: As you reviewed documents, if you found documents which might be exculpatory, could you tell us what you did with those?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, could I ask you to make a short break between question and answer and Ms. Bibles will do the same.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was trying, Your Honour. Exculpatory documents, any document that seemed to me in my reading as potentially exculpatory I would flag, I would notify the attorneys on the case, give them the ERN and a summary of the document or the reason why I saw it as exculpatory. And that's not only in my writing for this report but all of our research in the LRT. We always have that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Have any of these such documents changed your understanding of the patterns as you've described them throughout your report?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: No. My -- as I've continued to do my research, I have found further examples of what I have, but nothing that has changed my original understanding of the patterns, and the exculpatory documents might relate to particular incidents but not -- they did not change my understanding of the overall pattern.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, I would tender 65 ter 28454 or at least MFI it for these purposes at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In view of the -- what I understood to be a standing objection against the report, Mr. Stojanovic, the Chamber indicated that it would decide on the admission of the report once the witness had given her testimony. Do you still object?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour. In accordance with your decision that you have just read out, we are going to state our views once we've completed the cross-examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the report, 65 ter 28454 would receive number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P379, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification. Please proceed, Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Before we discuss some of the aspects of your report, I'd like to ask you about the term "Crisis Staff" as it's used in your report. Could you tell us what you're referring to when you used the term "Crisis Staff"?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: As I note in my report, I use it as an umbrella term for the municipal authorities acting in -- under emergency conditions, not the regular municipal assembly but a small emergency body claiming authority over the municipality, whether it be a Crisis Staff or War Presidency or war commission. All of those terms were used. They were slightly different -- there was an evolution in the terminology used, but all the sources I see emphasise the continuity between those terms, so from that -- from basing myself on that evidence, I use Crisis Staffs here as an umbrella term for War Presidencies and war commissions as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: From mid-to late May of 1992, were there changes in how the Bosnian Serb leadership viewed the municipal-level Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: I wouldn't say it was a change in how they viewed them but what we do see a formalisation of the status of the Crisis Staffs. We see even as the republic level organs are formalising the Bosnian Serb state and establishing the authority over other organs they've created, they're doing the same with the Crisis Staffs. As you see in my report, Crisis Staffs were originally formed within the SDS party as party organs, but we see in May 1992 in -- in an -- in a -- increasing a number of instructions formalising their role -- the role in the state of these Crisis Staffs and the authority of the republican level over them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm mindful of the clock and note that this would be a good time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Bibles, it is. Ms. Hanson, before we adjourn, I'd like to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony or communicate in any other way with whomever about your testimony, whether that is testimony - as it little as it may be - given already today or still to be given tomorrow and perhaps the day after tomorrow. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30, but not in this courtroom but in courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: II?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Courtroom II, yes. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day and we'll resume tomorrow, Tuesday, the 30th of October, at 9.30 in the morning, in Courtroom II.
